newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND--US Treasury yield curve seen steady in 97.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND--US Treasury yield curve seen steady in 97.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury yield curve looks to stay mostly flat in 1997, with the spread between the two-year note and the benchmark 30-year bond sticking between 75 and 100 basis points, Wall Street analysts said.
But the makeup of the curve should be different, they said, predicting that short- and long-term rates would edge down in tandem for both technical and fundamental reasons.
"The downside momentum (in yields) is in place and should continue until there is technical evidence it would not," said Ronald Daino, fixed income technical strategist at Smith Barney Inc.
At the same time, most analysts expect equally positive economic and inflation news aiding both ends of the curve.

"For the first time in my career we have had responsible fiscal and monetary policy taking place at the same time. I like that," said Stephen Slifer, chief financial markets economist at Lehman Brothers Inc. "If we can keep getting them right a lot of good things can happen with the economy.
"If the Fed keeps getting it right, there is no reason why we can't have six, seven, eight, nine or 10 years of expansion," he said.
There is, however, some disagreement as to which sector of the curve will do better next year.
Patrick Dimick, Treasury market strategist at UBS Securities LLC, figured the long end could outperform the short end, but by a slim margin.

"People are conscious where the front-end is trading relative to federal funds (now at 5.25 percent)," said Dimick. "Without some evidence the economy may be slowing at an alarming rate, I do not think two-year notes can do much better than 5.50 percent.
"You need to have people talking about the possibilty of a recession and an easing for the two-year to go to 5.25 percent" from its current 5.88 percent level, he added.
Economists, though, do not predict the economy to come close to a recession in 1997.
Economic growth, many forecast, should be in the 2.0 percent to 2.5 percent range with inflation remaining at a tame rate of below 3.0 percent.

But, analysts said, much depends on the consumer and the strength of the 1996 holiday shopping season, with the final results not expected until sometime in January. General sentiment is for a good -- not great -- shopping season. Also, the Federal Reserve is seen on hold for the time being.
Even with a steady Fed, some expect short-term Treasury yields to fall.

Craig Coats, co-head of taxable fixed income at Prudential Securities Inc, forecast a slight steepening in the curve to 100 basis points by mid-year, with the two-year yield falling to 5.0 percent and the 30-year bond to 6.0 percent.
"The dollar will do better so the focus will be on international buying of five-years and in," Coats said.

He said the short end should benefit from hopes of a balanced budget and lower entitlement spending if the government cuts cost of living adjustments as recommended in a recent report on flaws in the consumer price index.
Daino agreed that Treasury yields will fall in 1997.

"We are seeing that interest rate models suggest that in this turn right now, the long bond can go through 6.10 percent through 6.0 percent, approaching 5.50 percent in 1997," Daino said, adding that short maturities should decline a comparable amount.

He did not offer a timetable for the dive in yields or how far yields can fall. But he said "the most important thing isn't levels but direction ... And the direction is most definitely down for rates into 1997 ... at least for the first six months" of the year.

A yield curve spread of 75 to 100 basis points would be similar to most of 1996, when the spread between the two-year note and 30-year bond stayed between 70 and 90 basis points from mid-March through December. It widened only briefly as the market realized there would be no budget deficit pact, and thus no wave of cuts in official rates by the Federal Reserve.

The spread began 1996 at 79 basis points (with the two-year note at 5.18 percent and the 30-year bond at 5.97 percent). If the market remains stable, the spread will end 1996 around 80 basis points, as the two-year note trades at 5.88 percent and the bond at 6.68 percent.

While most believe current levels are at the upper part of the range, a handful of bond bears see rates going even higher, given some probability inflation will pickup in early 1997 due to wage pressures spilling over into consumer prices.

"There will be an almost equal degree of pressure on short-term coupons as bonds in 1997," said William Sullivan, director of money market research at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc, who predicted the long bond yield will hit 7.50 percent and the two-year will rise to 6.50 percent sometime next year. "I do not see a dramatic and sustained shift to the yield curve.

"As the economy gains momentum and the Fed is forced to tighten policy, yields in two-, five- and 10-year notes will go up as much as the bond," said Sullivan, who forecasts 50 basis points of tightening in 1997.
He said, though, that the risk to the forecast is that the yield curve will flatten -- although not substantially -- if the market senses Fed policymakers will raise rates more than they actually do.

Analysts noted that while the yield curve spread should remain 75 to 100 basis points, there could be times when it is either flatter or steeper. But when the year is out, the spread should be as flat as it was at the end of 1995 and 1996.
"It is truly a boring scenario," Slifer of Lehman said. "We will get some wiggles and the curve could move around, but I don't feel like we are going anywhere on a sustained basis."
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212 859-1867))
